issues.description: The Latin 'unicuique eorum' means 'to each of them' (referring to the recipients), but the translation 'each granted them' incorrectly makes 'each' refer to the kings (the subjects).
The Latin 'muro incluso' means 'enclosed by a wall' or 'walled up'; the specific addition of 'in a tomb' is not in the source text.
The translation omits 'taliter ut' (in such a way that / so that), turning a result clause into a coordinate thought, though the core meaning is preserved.
The Latin 'plausibilis' here means 'pleasing', 'acceptable', or 'praiseworthy'. Translating it as 'plausible' is a false friend in modern English, though it was used this way in early modern English.

issues.span: while the blessed apostle John was laboring
issues.description: The Latin 'a beato Johanne apostolo... insudante' indicates the agent of the passive verb 'delegatus est' (appointed by the blessed apostle John, who was laboring...). The translation renders it as a temporal clause, losing the agency.
The Latin 'ipsi' is dative and agrees with 'prædicationi' (the preaching itself), rather than being a nominative pronoun ('himself') referring to John.
The Latin 'dederunt' simply means 'gave'; the addition of 'each' changes the meaning to imply each king gave twelve portions, rather than the three kings collectively giving twelve portions.

issues.span: by the Spaniards, the Scots, and the French against the English
issues.description: The translation reverses the roles of the English and the other nations. The Latin 'ab Anglis' means 'by the English', and 'adversus Hispanos, Scotos et Gallos' means 'against the Spaniards, Scots, and French'.
The Latin 'dicit' means 'says' or 'asserts', not 'denies' (which would be 'negat'). This reverses the meaning of the legal maxim.
The Latin 'Caiphæ' refers to Caiaphas, not Pilate.
The Latin 'latere' means 'side', not 'hands'.

The Latin 'cum ... accepissent' is a cum-clause with the pluperfect subjunctive, meaning 'when they had received' or 'having received'. Translating it as 'in order to receive' incorrectly changes the temporal/causal relationship of the events.
The Latin 'ita ... ut' introduces a result clause ('in such a way ... that' or 'so ... that'), but the translation uses 'because', which changes the logical relationship.
The Latin word 'duntaxat' (only, merely, at least) is omitted from the translation.
The Latin 'duntaxat' (only, at least) is omitted from the translation.
The phrasing is slightly awkward; 'the word of the Gospel' would be a more natural rendering of 'Evangelii sermo'.

The Latin 'cum' here introduces a causal or temporal clause ('since' or 'when'), not a concessive one ('although'), as his continued preaching is the reason for his re-imprisonment, not something that happened in spite of it.
While a literal translation of 'inclusus', in the context of being locked up by the Jews, 'imprisoned' or 'confined' would be more natural.
The Latin 'dicatur' means 'is said' or 'is reported', whereas 'is known' implies certainty (which would be 'scitur' or 'constat').
The word 'reliably' is added; the Latin 'est proditum' simply means 'it has been reported' or 'handed down'.
In the context of textual transmission, 'exemplaribus' refers to 'copies' or 'manuscripts', rather than 'examples'.
The Latin 'officio' refers to a liturgical office or rite, not a 'council' (which would be 'concilio').
The Latin 'ad Henricum Blesensem' means the preface was addressed 'to Henry of Blois', not written 'by' him.
The Latin 'a sanctis apostolis' means 'by the holy apostles' (indicating the agent of the passive verb), not 'for the holy apostles'.
The Latin 'a Malmesburiensi citatus' is a passive construction meaning 'cited by Malmesbury', not 'citing Malmesbury'.
Missing terminal punctuation at the end of the sentence.

issues.span: in whose time Christ Jesus was born of the Virgin Mary, son of Kimbelinus king of the Britons
issues.description: The translation misplaces the appositive 'filio Kimbelini regis Britonum', making it appear that Christ Jesus (or the Virgin Mary) was the son of Kimbelinus, whereas in the Latin it modifies King Arviragus.
Translates 'ad Timotheum' (to Timothy) as 'of Timothy', incorrectly implying Timothy is the author rather than the recipient.

issues.span: which had been brought to him
issues.description: The Latin 'quas secum... detulerat' is active and means 'which he had brought with him', not passive 'which had been brought to him'.
The Latin 'damno dilectorum nobis in Christo' means 'damage to our beloved in Christ' (objective genitive), not 'damage from'.
The Latin 'VI. Calendas Augusti' refers to the sixth day before the Kalends of August (July 27), not after.
The Latin 'breviario' refers to the Breviary, not the Missal (which would be 'missale').

issues.span: Peter suffered martyrdom while James was still alive.
issues.description: The translation reverses the roles of Peter and James. The Latin 'Jacobus martyrium subiit vivente Petro' means 'James suffered martyrdom while Peter was alive'.
The translation introduces 'Peter' as the subject of the preaching, whereas the Latin 'prædicavit' refers back to Joseph of Arimathea. There is no mention of Peter in the Latin text.
The Latin 'Timotheum' means 'Timothy', not 'Paul'.

issues.span: Linus was the father of a certain Herculanus
issues.description: The Latin 'Patrem ... Lini Herculanum quendam fuisse' means that a certain Herculanus was the father of Linus, not that Linus was the father of Herculanus. The translation reverses the genealogical relationship.
The Latin word 'post' means 'after', but it was incorrectly translated as 'before', which completely changes the historical timeline.

issues.span: after the Lord went to his passion
issues.description: The Latin 'Domino passionem adeunte' uses a present participle in an ablative absolute, meaning 'when the Lord was approaching his passion' or 'at the time of the Lord's passion', not 'after'.
The Latin 'fuerat' is pluperfect ('had been' or 'was'), indicating he was already a senator at that time, not that he 'became' one afterwards.

issues.span: twenty-three years in the East, but passed twelve years at Rome
issues.description: The translation swaps the numbers. The Latin states 12 years in the East ('duodecim... in oriente') and 23 years at Rome ('viginti autem et tres... Romæ').
The Latin 'ullo' means 'any', not 'all'. The phrase 'nec... ab ullo' means 'nor... by any' (i.e., by none), whereas 'nor... by all' implies it might have been done by some.
The Latin 'Nemo' means 'no one', not 'not all'. This reverses the meaning of the sentence.
The Latin 'unquam' (ever) is omitted from the translation.
The translation completely omits the introductory phrase 'Hinc Arnobius' (Hence Arnobius [says]).
The Latin 'cum' in this context is concessive ('although' or 'whereas'), not causal ('because').
The translation completely omits the introductory phrase 'Hinc Arnobius' (Hence Arnobius) from the Latin source.

issues.span: I have abused both my own leisure and the reader's patience in rehearsing
issues.description: The Latin 'abutar, si ... commemorem' is a conditional ('I would abuse... if I were to recount'), but the translation renders it as a completed past action ('I have abused... in rehearsing').
The Latin 'si' means 'if', not 'since'. This changes a conditional statement into a factual one.
The Latin 'fuisset' is a pluperfect subjunctive ('would have been'), which forms the apodosis of the conditional sentence. Translating it as 'was' loses the conditional meaning.
The Latin 'cognoscimus' is first-person plural ('we know' or 'we learn'), but is translated here as singular.
The Latin 'Hunc Mevinum Britannum chronographum appellat' more accurately translates to 'calls this Mevinus a British chronographer', whereas the translation reverses the object and complement.
The Latin 'eum' is the direct object of 'separat' ('separates him'), but the translation adds 'them from', altering the grammatical structure and meaning.
The Latin 'illo' refers to Plutarch (mentioned just before as 'is'), meaning she lived in the same age as him. The translator has incorrectly substituted 'Pudens'.
The emphatic particle 'utique' (certainly / to be sure) is omitted in the translation.
Strictly speaking, the pronoun should be in the nominative case ('as he') in this comparative clause, though 'as him' is common in modern usage.
